reference.source: GeneReviews / WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
clinicalPearls: The syndrome predisposes to multiple schwannomas along peripheral, spinal, and cranial nerves while characteristically sparing the vestibular nerves bilaterally, which distinguishes it from neurofibromatosis type 2
Chronic, often severe neuropathic pain is the dominant symptom and may be disproportionate to the size or number of tumours
The two principal genes are SMARCB1 and LZTR1, both located on chromosome 22 near the NF2 locus, and a proportion of patients have no identified variant
A single unilateral vestibular schwannoma or isolated meningiomas can occur, so careful imaging and phenotyping are needed to separate it from NF2
Tumours are histologically benign, and malignant transformation is rare, so surveillance and symptom control rather than aggressive resection guide management
Diagnosis rests on clinical criteria, imaging demonstrating multiple schwannomas, histological confirmation, and molecular genetic testing including tumour analysis
Care is multidisciplinary, combining neurosurgery or peripheral nerve surgery for symptomatic or enlarging lesions with dedicated chronic pain management
reference.pathophysiology: Schwannomatosis is a tumour predisposition syndrome caused by germline variants in the tumour suppressor genes SMARCB1 or LZTR1, both situated on chromosome 22q close to NF2. Tumour development typically follows a multi-hit mechanism in which the germline variant is compounded by somatic loss of the region encompassing both the predisposing gene and NF2, so that the resulting schwannomas show combined inactivation. This shared chromosomal neighbourhood explains the clinical overlap with NF2 while the preservation of at least one functional NF2 allele in constitutional tissue accounts for the absence of the bilateral vestibular schwannomas that define NF2. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, and many cases appear sporadic.
additionalDifferentials: Localised chronic pain syndromes without tumour
additionalInvestigations: Whole-neuraxis MRI (brain including internal auditory meati, and whole spine) to map tumours and exclude bilateral vestibular schwannomas
MRI of symptomatic peripheral nerves or plexuses
Histological confirmation of resected lesions as schwannomas
Molecular genetic testing of SMARCB1 and LZTR1, ideally including tumour tissue analysis
Audiological assessment if any vestibulocochlear symptoms are present
redFlags: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, which point to NF2 rather than schwannomatosis
Rapid tumour growth, new neurological deficit, or features suggesting malignant transformation
Spinal cord or cauda equina compression from an enlarging intraspinal schwannoma
Intractable pain with functional decline requiring specialist intervention
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is generally normal because the tumours are benign and malignant change is uncommon. The principal burden is chronic pain and the cumulative morbidity of multiple tumours and their surgical treatment; quality of life depends heavily on effective pain control and judicious, function-preserving surgery.
pitfalls: Diagnosing schwannomatosis without excluding bilateral vestibular schwannomas and thereby missing NF2
Assuming pain is proportional to tumour bulk and under-treating disabling neuropathic pain
Pursuing aggressive resection of all tumours rather than targeting symptomatic or growing lesions
Relying on blood testing alone, since tumour tissue analysis often clarifies the genetic diagnosis
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
